name: Dusty amber
lede: Dusty amber is a warm, muted gold, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Kariyasu, named for a grass rather than the fossil resin its English name suggests.

sections.title: The color of a dye grass
sections.body:
Kariyasu (苅安) is named in the Wikipedia list of Japan's traditional colors for Japanese triandra grass (*Themeda japonica*), not for the fossil resin amber that gives the English name here [1]. Beyond that identification, the page gives no further history for the name, and it is undocumented in the sources consulted here [1].

Its nearest named neighbors on file are [[primuline-yellow]], 2.6 units off, and [[goldenrod]], 3.4 off [2], close enough on screen that a grass and a mineral resin can land on the same gold.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within six units of this swatch in 329 of 23,781 paintings, 1.38 percent, as photographed, with the within-painting lens finding it in the same 329 [3]. That makes it more common than 78 percent of the named colors in our library [3]. It peaks in the 1300s, present in 3.2 percent of our 251 paintings from that century, 1.7 times the museums' baseline rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 72 percent of its 329 appearances by lightness rank [3].

George Dawe is its most devoted painter on file, present in 11 of his 50 works here, more than seven times the baseline rate for the museums that hold them [3]. The earliest match, by Bonaventura Berlinghieri, dates to 1250, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. It is most over-represented in paintings from India, and shares canvases with [[dark-goldenrod|Dark Goldenrod]] and [[bistre-brown|Bistre Brown]] far more often than chance [3]. These are computed color matches to photographed, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [3].
